title: Phonetics · L2 Organs of speech and articulation

questions.stem: Match each speech subsystem to its role:
options: Articulatory — shapes the airstream into consonants and vowels
Phonatory — shapes the airstream in the mouth and nose
Respiratory — supplies the power source (lungs push air out)
Phonatory — larynx and vocal folds modulate the airstream and produce voicing
questions.explanation: Shaping in the throat, mouth and nose is the articulatory system's job.

questions.stem: A sound is voiced when the vocal folds:
options: Are drawn together
Vibrate as air passes between them
Remain apart
Close the nasal cavity
questions.explanation: Apart and not vibrating = voiceless. The nasal cavity is closed by the soft palate.

questions.stem: Which pairs are distinguished only by voicing, according to the lecture?
options: /m/ and /n/
/s/ and /z/
/p/ and /s/
/p/ and /b/
questions.explanation: Voicing separates pairs that are otherwise identical, such as /p/–/b/ and /s/–/z/.

options: Upper teeth
Hard palate
Soft palate
Alveolar ridge
questions.explanation: Passive: upper lip, upper teeth, alveolar ridge, hard palate, rear wall of the pharynx. The soft palate is active.

options: Tongue
Lower lip
Soft palate (velum)
Lower jaw
questions.explanation: Active articulators move toward a fixed surface to form a constriction or closure: lower lip, tongue, lower jaw, soft palate.

options: Passive articulators provide a relatively fixed surface
They are located above the larynx
The rear wall of the pharynx is an active articulator
Active articulators move toward that surface to form a constriction or closure
questions.explanation: The rear wall of the pharynx is passive.

questions.stem: The five regions of the tongue are:
options: tip, blade, front, back, root
tip, blade, palate, back, root
tip, body, dorsum, uvula, root
apex, front, middle, back, epiglottis
questions.explanation: The blade is just behind the tip. The uvula, epiglottis and palate are not parts of the tongue.

options: Different sounds are made by raising different parts of it toward the roof of the mouth
It is involved in most English sounds
It is the most flexible and important articulator
It is a passive articulator
questions.explanation: The tongue is the most mobile, active articulator.

questions.stem: When the soft palate (velum) is lowered:
options: A nasal sound such as /m/, /n/ or /ŋ/ is produced
Air escapes only through the mouth
Air can pass through the nose
The nasal cavity is sealed off
questions.explanation: Raised velum → nasal cavity sealed, air through the mouth only → oral sound.

questions.stem: Match the articulator to its function (lecture's Table 1):
options: Alveolar ridge — target for tongue-tip closure or narrowing
Lower lip — fixed surface for dental contact
Soft palate — opens or closes the nasal cavity
Hard palate — surface for tongue-front raising
questions.explanation: The lower lip is active: it moves toward the teeth or upper lip. The upper lip/teeth are the fixed surfaces.

questions.stem: Which statement explains the role of the soft palate?
options: It is the passive target for tongue-tip closure
It acts as a valve that distinguishes oral from nasal sounds
It produces voicing
It is the power source of speech
questions.explanation: Voicing = vocal folds; power = lungs; tongue-tip target = alveolar ridge.
